cells.tense: Release is moving through your days without needing to be pushed.
cells.ask: Take the task you keep almost-finishing, do its last hour today, and mark it done on paper.
cells.core:
Endings come out of your hands clean right now. You close something and the closing itself makes room — not staring at the door, not holding it shut. That's rare, and it's doing quiet work: new things have somewhere to land because the old ones aren't still sitting in your lap.

What keeps this is tending without clutching. A plant doesn't need you standing over it; it needs water, light, and then your absence. Give what you've made what it needs to hold up on its own, then step back and let it be enough. The test isn't whether you feel finished. It's whether you can stop working on something and let the next thing show up in its own time, without earning the right to rest first.
cells.sheetLine: You can close a thing and mean it.
cells.verb: letting go of what no longer holds
cells.place: the point where the work is done and the next thing begins

cells.tense: You will be handing it off before it is finished, once the moment comes.
cells.ask: Take the project you keep wanting to hand off early, work twenty unhurried minutes on it alone tomorrow, then stop on purpose.
cells.core:
You're jumping to the ending before the middle is done. Somewhere ahead is the version where it's over and you're already living there — announcing it, passing it on, releasing something that still needs your hands. The gesture reads as trust from the outside. From the inside, it's a sprint past the part that would require you to sit still and finish.

What turns this is quiet practice: twenty minutes, no audience, repetition instead of announcement. Keep one small light on rather than torching it. If you can work without a witness, the thing gets to be whole before you offer it up. Releasing it isn't the problem. Doing it before the work is ready is.

cells.tense: You were carrying it then, and your hands have not opened since.
cells.ask: Pick one thing you're keeping alive past its time, hold it deliberately for five minutes, then set it down for an hour and watch your body do it.
cells.core:
Something is being carried that's ready to be put down. The grip is tired — it shows in your shoulders before it shows in your words — and it keeps going, past the point where it was useful. Things that might have ended stay held open, and what's exhausted is you, not the thing.

Opening your hands for good isn't the move yet. The move is to grip one thing on purpose, so it becomes something you're doing rather than something happening to you. Five minutes of deliberate hold, then an hour of deliberate rest. Your body learns the difference between the two. One hour is enough to start, and starting is what makes the rest possible later.

cells.tense: You have already put something down and you don't count it as done.
cells.ask: Find one thing you say you still have to do, and write one sentence on whether you stopped doing it or already finished it.
cells.core:
You speak of it as still open. Look at what you actually reach for and what you quietly stopped reaching for — the answer is already there, and you've been living it while telling people you haven't decided. The message you didn't send, the person you stopped mentioning, the evening that no longer goes that way. Something was released without an announcement, and now you can't tell whether it ended or just went quiet.

Care for what's still growing means looking at what you do, not what you say you're waiting on. One sentence, written plainly, draws the line. The release already happened. Knowing it is the part you can add today.
